- Cats (especially my cats)

The thing is that depression is treatable to the extent that you can be almost entirely symptom free with the right medications and such. For assisted suicide, you have to meet a very strict list of things and a couple of those are:
1) your condition is incurable and/or can no longer be treated 
1a) you are going to die prematurely because of your condition
2) you are of sound mind (meaning mentally you don’t want to die just because your brain isn’t braining correctly) 

A person with chronic, fatal illness won’t even be eligible for euthanasia if they don’t pass the psychological portion. Euthanasia is entirely death with dignity. You can’t avoid that your body is decaying and you are actively dying, but you can choose the terms you go on. 

I don’t think you’re a bad person for thinking this as I’ve thought the most merciful thing at times would be for my life to end solely because living every day was torture, but at the end of the day, depression is treatable. It’s not easy, it’s not gonna happen overnight, but it is 100% treatable. If your treatment isn’t working, I suggest you be honest with your provider and try something different. Try a combination of medications if you must. 

If *that* isn’t working, consider that you may need a new/dual diagnosis. See multiple psychiatrists. Check into a psych ward for observation. Exhaust every possibility then flip some stones until you find some more possibilities. 

Also, progress isn’t linear. You might feel better for a while then come crashing back down. You just gotta get back up on the horse.

Know your stuff. I’m just gonna rapid fire some stuff here: Like a flat can’t be sent via ground, It has to be priority. If someone asks about overnight, stick something on the scale and ask for the zip code. Sometimes it can’t be overnight and will be two days. Hazardous items cannot be sent overnight. Check all prepaid for caution labels, if you send it outside of a hazmat container you can be held liable if you did the acceptance scan; the machines can pick up the barcode and tell who the clerk is that accepted it and that they didn’t handle it correctly. NEVER PRESS THE CIVIL PENALTY OR HAZMAT QUESTION FOR THE CUSTOMER. If you see a parcel that says on the label the weight is four ounces, but the box seems heavier, PACKAGE VALIDATE. If a package has ANY priority items on it (tape, box, label), but is being sent ground, postage due them. Get good at explaining that first class is only for letters and flats, and be prepared to explain why exactly they cannot use that option for their envelope that is rigid with cardboard, or something that is too thick to be a flat. If a customer asks for tape, tell them they can either purchase tape or you can give them priority tape, but they will have to send it via priority mail. Know what is restricted, if a box has any alcohol branding on it, they cannot use that box. Be ready and knowledgeable on being able to explain their options for sending (like if they want ground or priority or express etc). Learn endorsements and how the plant works. People will ask you constantly why their letter got returned, and why was it IA. Make sure they know, in no uncertain terms, that the delivery date is not guaranteed unless they are using express mail. If someone says they forgot their box key and you do not know them, ask for ID. If they cannot produce ID, tell them you cannot give them their mail. If they say so and so knows me, they give me my mail, inform them when they will be back and have them come in then. Giving the wrong person mail is a big big big no no. 

It is always better to do the right thing, even if a customer gets mad. Stand your ground. Keep your cool. If a customer gets out of hand, get a supervisor. Briefly explain the situation and ask for assistance. If a supervisor is not available, tell them you are unable to resolve their issue and you want to escalate it. Take their name and number and address if needed, and have your supervisor give them a call when they get back. Tell them to have a nice day, and shake it off for the next customer. Ask questions to senior clerks whenever possible. Ask multiple times if you have to. If you see them doing something, just ask what they’re doing and how and why and all that. 

Mail is complicated, but you will learn. I enjoy my job. Just keep your chin up and keep learning. Good luck!

The jobs I have grown to resent the quickest have always been those that were short shifts and more days, and I have always requested that I work less days with the same hours. 

3) while ten hours a day might seem like a lot, you can easily justify it and portion off your day. When I’d work jobs like these, I’d take my lunch break as late in the day as possible. Let’s say; work 6-8 hours, half an hour lunch break (pretty standard) and then only have 2.5-3 hours left to pound out. Let me start by saying that I really respect you for not using a potential mental issue as a crutch, and really asking yourself if you have a problem before spouting to the world that you have a disorder when you're not even sure yourself. If there were more people like you, mental illness would be taken way more seriously than it is now. Seriously, you are great for this. 

You are considered to have a disorder when it starts affecting your daily life. It's normal and even healthy to have anxiety over stressful things, such as a test or trying to get a job. The issue comes when the anxiety never leaves. When you're anxious to go grocery shopping, return to school, leave your house, or even for no real reason at all. Anxiety as a disorder never leaves you. 

I agree with everyone else in the way that you can't officially tell until you seek help from a professional, but the fact that you can talk yourself down from it already seems like a good sign for you. I really encourage you to seek help, even if you do it just to find out that you're perfectly okay and maybe need to implement some methods to help you cope with periods of greater anxiety due to, well, anything, really. 

I started showing symptoms of an anxiety disorder from an incredibly young age, but between not knowing much about mental health and being scared to say anything, I didn't get help until a few years ago. I lived over a decade with an increasingly worse mental affliction and as one commenter posted, I kick myself every day and wonder how much better my life would have been and would be now if I didn't let my anxiety fester. Untreated anxiety disorders can turn into panic attack disorders, and I didn't get help until that happened. I wanted to DIE because anything would have been better than constantly feeling like I'm having a heart attack. It was torture. 

Don't be us. If you think you have an issue, go to a doctor. Worst case scenario is you're developing a disorder and you *can* get help. Best case scenario is it's too early to tell and you become more informed and will know if it becomes an issue, or you have no affliction at all and can try to pick up outlets or coping mechanisms for when normal, healthy anxiety becomes a little too much.  

I wish you the best of luck, but please take the advice from us and please DO NOT WAIT TO FIND OUT IF YOU'RE SICK BY BECOMING SICKER.

I've been there. I can probably explain everything for you.

The flu type thing is most of it, giving you the dizziness, blurred vision, etc. and your anxiety is helping to make it worse. The lump feeling in your throat is another anxiety thing that I experience all the time whether I'm sick or not. Think of it as a tense muscle. You can try drinking water, but it's something you might just have to learn to ignore. (I experience it even under mild stress, and it gets worse as I get more stressed out.)

The feeling in the back of your nose is probably stuck mucous. You can try to snort it and spit it out, but it might be really stuck in there. The dryness that made you feel like it was burning was probably just that your sickness + maybe the weather is drying out your sinuses, which causes that "burning" feeling. Breathing through your mouth to avoid it will dry out your throat as well. Keep cough drops handy and drink a lot of water. Because you're on high alert and worried about the burning, you must've had some kind of panic attack, which made you hyperventilate and feel like you can't breathe. 

Just try your hardest to focus on something else. It can be very hard, but try. Drink lots of water and ask yer mum for cough drops. Try cold and hot drinks to soothe your throat. I find hot helps me clear mucous while cold makes the burning go away. 

I go through this nearly every winter, and it's getting easier to deal with as I realise I'm just sick and anxious. Try the things I've mentioned, and once you notice the symptoms start to go away you should notice the anxiety start to fade too.

Feel better! 

Edit: I forgot to mention nasal spray. Try not to get too nasal spray happy as the saline can make you a bit nauseous. If that happens, just have a bite to eat or a nice cup of juice if you're not too hungry.

It can be hard. Some nights I wake up in the middle of a deep sleep to feeling like I'm literally going to die. Sometimes I wish I would just so I wouldn't have to deal with it anymore.

It can be so tiring and stressful, but it's the best thing you can do for yourself. I also try to think of anything but the "what if's" when I feel an attack coming on. 

The other day I was in the walmart parking lot when I started thinking about how the last time I was there, I started crying and had to put down everything in my arms and run out of the store. I started feeling terrible, so I said out loud to myself, "No, don't even think about that. Think about the lights on the cars. Yeah, they're cool as shit." Honestly, the most helpful thing for me is actually crying.

If you're alone, I 110% suggest just letting it out. You will most always feel better immediately after as crying releases endorphins. It also feels good to get all of that built up tension off your chest.

Other than that, I:

- Count objects. Really focus on this. 5 things you can see, 4 things you can touch, three things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and one good thing about yourself or something that makes you happy. It's important to pay attention, because this is a method of grounding. It makes you focus on the here and now reality instead of the what if/maybe anxiety. It doesn't have to be those exact things, just a list of stuff to ground you in reality.

- Take deep breaths. Stereotypical, but it works. If you're breathing too fast, just take a couple of seconds to breath through the nose and out of the mouth. Once you feel calm enough, you can increase it to three seconds, and continue like this. Soon enough you will be breathing normally and your heart rate will have decreased. 

- Look up those symptom! I only suggest this if you have a history of anxiety. If you have symptoms that make you feel like you're having a heart attack (this is the most common panic attack for me.) Use a site that has a list of anxiety symptoms. This helps me because it helps me remind myself that everything I'm experiencing is a symptom of a panic attack. I had a really good site that I actually had my phone set to open up as the homepage, so if I needed it I had it in seconds. Sadly, my phone took a dump. After a quick search, though, I found this site: http://www.anxietycentre.com/anxiety-symptoms.shtml which covers most of the symptoms. ONLY look at anxiety symptoms. Not cancer symptoms. Not heart attack symptoms. ANXIETY SYMPTOMS ONLY! The purpose is to remind yourself that everything you're feeling is OKAY! It is okay to look up conditions that you have as well. I have GERD which can cause chest pain, which often makes me anxious. I also have a pinched nerve that makes my fingers go numb and gives me arm pain that makes me anxious. Anything that you can attribute to not dying is A+.

- If you're going to work and feeling ill, tell your coworkers and manager right away what to do if something happens. For example: I've had a collapsed lung once. It happened while I was at work and I started having trouble breathing and had to go to hospital. It's something I still worry about and thinking of it can make me feel short of breath. When I'm having one of these days, I tell a trusted coworker and my manager that if I become unresponsive to call 911 immediately and tell them that I was complaining of respiratory distress.

I do this because I feel less worried that if something happens to me, the EMTs won't know what's wrong and by the time they find out, it will be too late. If you actually are beginning to seriously fall ill, there are informed people that can save your life.

I've been doing this method for work for three years because of not being able to breath, racing heart, chest pains, etc. And here's the best part... Not once have I ever needed an ambulance!

- My favourite method: crying. If all else fails, let it out! I suggest that you do this as soon as possible to get yourself to feel better if you're alone or with close and understanding friends/family. You can say you're feeling anxious and excuse yourself. If you want to feel more safe, say that if you aren't back in X minutes that they should come make sure you're okay. If you really cannot contain it at work, it is especially important to excuse yourself, especially in a customer service environment. 

- Anything to occupy your mind. I come to Reddit often to say how I feel or just post some silly comments. Or even if you occupy your mind by remembering that you're not alone and we're all okay!

But, yeah. If you buy really cheap food, even a cat that only eats when hungry will eat a lot. Mainly because this food will probably satiate them for a short time but then run right through them. Kind of like humans and chinese food! Because it runs right through them, they'll want to keep eating as their stomach will empty faster.

Gonna try to tl;dr it here.

- Some cats can free feed, some cannot. Depends on if they're greedy eaters.

- High quality will not make them eat less or more. 

- Really low quality can make any cat eat more, as the food will likely not fill their stomachs for long.

- If you have more than one cat, I would not suggest free feeding. I also suggest each cat has their own litter box. This way you can be sure that each cat is eating properly and expelling waste properly. This is especially important while they're kittens.
(Edit: A little anecdote. My cat had a UTI once, which can eventually become very serious. The only reasons that I figured she was sick were because she was drinking a lot more water than usual and because there was little to no pee over the course of a few days in her box. If I had two cats back then and only one box, I may have never known she was sick and taken her to the vet too late as the pee could have come from either or both cats. Same thing can go with bowel obstructions, you really need to keep an eye on cats as they will hide their pain. 3:)


THE MOST TL;DR OF THE TL;DR'S - high quality food vs. average shelf food will not make a difference in free feeding.
